polarcodec benchmark report

30 real Telegram circles, 14 arms under x264 and three under AV1, six quality settings each. Bytes at equal disc quality relative to the plain square.

How to read these tables. Every row is one way of feeding a round video to the codec (an "arm"); square is the plain square file that Telegram already uses, so it is the baseline at 0. The number that matters is the BD-rate: how many extra bytes an arm needs to reach the same picture quality as the square, as a percentage, across the whole quality range. +81.7 means "1.8 times the bytes"; a negative value would mean fewer bytes than the square, i.e. a win. median is the typical clip, the 95 % CI is the range the true median is likely in, and wins counts the clips on which that arm was the cheapest. Polar arms start with polar_; ellip_ and sc_ are disc-to-square maps; the square_post_, square_warp_ and square_up_ rows are controls that isolate the cost of resampling and of the extra pixels. Below the summary come the same-bitrate check, timings, aggregate rate-distortion curves, transform-only floors, and one section per clip. The last section, AV1, repeats the comparison under a newer codec (SVT-AV1, and libaom with its rotation and zoom tools switched on and off): the same arms, the same clips, each codec against its own square.

  • metric definitions: PSNR-Y/SSIM-Y masked to the disc (r <= r_map - 1 = R + 1.5, R = W/2, r_map = R + 2.5 = the content radius the maps cover), inner (r <= 0.75 R), rim (disc minus inner); psnr_edge = the anti-aliased content edge r_map - 1 < r <= r_map + 1 (clipped by the frame; the inverse maps synthesise it with a ramp to white); vmaf_disc = VMAF with everything outside the disc mask whitened in both frames; kbps = video stream bytes / encoded duration; BD-rate vs square (negative = fewer bits). mb_pad = extra area x264 codes because the canvas is not a multiple of 16. r_content = content radius detected on 3 frames of the source (non-white Y < 234 fraction per 0.5 px ring).
  • controls (dashed in the plots): square_post_<p> = square encode, decoded frames pushed through forward+inverse of <p> before measuring (does the inverse warp denoise?); square_warp_<p> = forward+inverse of <p> with no codec, then square encode (charges the resampling loss to a square encode); square_up_<p> = Lanczos-4 upscale to <p>'s canvas pixel count (up_side), encode, Lanczos-4 downscale (pixel-budget control). <arm>_noaa = anti-aliased forward remap forced off.

Summary: BD-rate vs square (percent, negative is better)

Median with a percentile-bootstrap 95 % CI (2000 resamples of the per-file values, seed 0), mean, IQR; wins = files on which the arm has the lowest BD-rate (square counts as 0). BD-rate fits log10(kbps) as a cubic in the metric per arm and integrates over the overlapping metric range; a file is dropped for an arm when the overlap is < 1 dB / 0.005 or the curve is not monotonic.

How they were measured (time.perf_counter, per cell, then divided by the frame count):

  • forward: sum over frames of the arm's to_canvas call in the encoding process (the map's forward remap with Lanczos-4 — two remaps plus a box filter when aa is on — or, for the controls, the pre-processing: warp round trip for square_warp_*, Lanczos upscale for square_up_*, a copy for square_post_*).
  • x264 encode: wall time of the writer from the encoder process start until the canvas file is closed, including the rgb24 pipe and the rgb->yuv420p conversion. The canvas frames are staged to a raw file before the encoder starts, so no transform time is inside this number (x264 -threads 2, -preset medium).
  • ffmpeg H.264 decode: wall time of one ffmpeg process decoding the canvas file to an rgb24 raw file (demux + H.264 decode + yuv420p->rgb24 with the pinned sws flags + file write).
  • inverse: sum over frames of from_canvas (inverse remap + edge ramp; for the controls the post-processing).
  • total encode = forward + x264 encode; total decode = ffmpeg H.264 decode + inverse.

The cells run inside the bench's worker pool (5 workers on this machine, each with 2 encoder threads plus the Python transform), so absolute numbers depend on the load; compare arms against square within the same run. Per-process ffmpeg start-up (~50 ms) is inside the encode and decode legs.

AV1

The same harness under AV1 instead of x264: results/batch2_svtav1 is the 30-clip run with SVT-AV1 (preset 6, PSNR tuning, three arms: square, polar_eq, ellip_full), its synth/ the synthetic motions under SVT-AV1, and results/aom_ablation the synthetic clips with libaom's global + warped motion on vs off. Every BD-rate below is against that codec's own square, so the x264 column repeats the table above and the AV1 column answers "does a newer codec change the verdict?". Negative = fewer bytes than the square at equal quality.

AV1 gap: x264 vs AV1 on the same harness

On real footage the polar canvas (polar_eq) needs 82 % more bytes than the plain square under x264 and 76 % more bytes under svtav1 (BD-rate +82 % / +76 %; negative would mean polar is cheaper). On fast rotation (3 deg/frame, the one motion a polar canvas turns into a plain shift) polar_eq needs 14 % fewer bytes under x264 and 34 % fewer bytes under svtav1 (BD-rate -14 % -> -34 %). Switching libaom's global + warped motion tools on and off shows what they do: the plain square needs 20 % more bytes on rotation with the warps off (about 16 % fewer with them), and the polar advantage on rotation goes from 32 % fewer bytes (warps off) to 21 % fewer bytes (warps on) — reduced by about a third. AV1's warps do not remove the polar rotation advantage; rotation is still the only motion where the polar canvas pays.

BD-rate vs square (percent, negative = fewer bytes at equal quality, psnr_disc), median over files with the bootstrap 95 % CI of the median.
